Reference: Heckman, Ichimura and Todd (1997)

Model Setting

The paper asks whether a nonexperimental evaluation of a prototypical job training programme can reproduce the impact estimates of a randomized social experiment, and which features of the data and of the estimator matter for that. It uses the National JTPA (Job Training Partnership Act) experiment, whose randomized-out controls reveal the counterfactual no-training earnings of participants, together with three nonexperimental comparison groups: eligible nonparticipants (ENPs) living in the same local labour markets and interviewed with the same questionnaire, JTPA-eligible persons from the national SIPP survey, and no-shows who were accepted but never enrolled. Since neither controls nor comparison persons are treated, any difference between them, after an estimator has been applied, is a direct measure of that estimator's bias. The method is a two-stage strategy: estimate the probability of participation P(X)P(X)P(X) with a logit, then use it in kernel-based extensions of classical matching (local linear, regression-adjusted and a new conditional difference-in-differences matching estimator), whose asymptotic theory is developed in the companion paper by the same authors. The paper also shows that the weaker assumption of conditional mean independence, not full independence, is all that matching on the mean needs.

The main findings are three. First, the conventional measure of bias (the raw mean difference between controls and comparison persons) decomposes into a part due to non-overlapping support, a part due to misweighting on the common support, and selection bias rigorously defined; the first two dominate, and for adult males the raw bias of −342-342−342 dollars per month splits into 218 from non-overlap, −584-584−584 from density weighting and only 23 from selection on unobservables. Second, selection bias proper is nonetheless a sizeable fraction of the experimental impact (for adult males the average bias of 38 dollars is 87 percent of the impact), the assumptions that justify matching (conditional independence and conditional mean independence) are rejected for most groups, while the identifying assumption of difference-in-differences matching is not rejected for any group. Third, data quality matters as much as the method: comparison persons must live in the same local labour market, answer the same questionnaire and be described by recent labour force histories; geographic mismatch or survey mismatch (SIPP) produces biases of 100 to 240 dollars per month, of the same order as the raw biases in LaLonde (1986).

The Evaluation Problem

There are two potential states, “1” (treatment) and “0” (no treatment), with outcomes (Y1,Y0)(Y_1,Y_0)(Y1​,Y0​), and D=1D=1D=1 if a person is in state 1. The observed outcome is

Y=DY1+(1−D)Y0(1)Y=DY_1+(1-D)Y_0 \tag{1}Y=DY1​+(1−D)Y0​(1)

which is the Fisher, Roy or switching regression (Quandt 1972) model. The gain from participation is Δ=Y1−Y0\Delta=Y_1-Y_0Δ=Y1​−Y0​, which is never observed for anyone. Writing outcomes as functions of observables XXX and unobservables (U1,U0)(U_1,U_0)(U1​,U0​):

Y1=g1(X)+U1Y0=g0(X)+U0(2)\begin{aligned} Y_1&=g_1(X)+U_1\\ Y_0&=g_0(X)+U_0 \end{aligned} \tag{2}Y1​Y0​​=g1​(X)+U1​=g0​(X)+U0​​(2)

Conventional econometrics assumes E(U1∣X)=0E(U_1\mid X)=0E(U1​∣X)=0 and E(U0∣X)=0E(U_0\mid X)=0E(U0​∣X)=0 with g1(X)=Xβ1g_1(X)=X\beta_1g1​(X)=Xβ1​ and g0(X)=Xβ0g_0(X)=X\beta_0g0​(X)=Xβ0​, but matching requires neither exogeneity nor linearity. The parameter of interest is the mean effect of treatment on the treated (TT):

E(Y1−Y0∣X,D=1)=E(Δ∣X,D=1)=g1(X)−g0(X)+E(U1−U0∣X,D=1)(3)E(Y_1-Y_0\mid X,D=1)=E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)=g_1(X)-g_0(X)+E(U_1-U_0\mid X,D=1) \tag{3}E(Y1​−Y0​∣X,D=1)=E(Δ∣X,D=1)=g1​(X)−g0​(X)+E(U1​−U0​∣X,D=1)(3)

which combines “structure” g1−g0g_1-g_0g1​−g0​ with the means of the error terms among participants. The matching estimators estimate its average over a subset SSS of the support of XXX given D=1D=1D=1:

M(S)=∫SE(Δ∣X,D=1) dF(X∣D=1)∫SdF(X∣D=1)(4)M(S)=\frac{\int_SE(\Delta\mid X,D=1)\,dF(X\mid D=1)}{\int_SdF(X\mid D=1)} \tag{4}M(S)=∫S​dF(X∣D=1)∫S​E(Δ∣X,D=1)dF(X∣D=1)​(4)

M(S)M(S)M(S) is the gross gain of participants relative to what they would have earned without the programme and, set against costs, answers whether an existing programme should be kept. Randomization among accepted applicants, with R=1R=1R=1 for persons randomized in and R=0R=0R=0 for persons randomized out, gives Y=D[RY1+(1−R)Y0]+(1−D)Y0Y=D[RY_1+(1-R)Y_0]+(1-D)Y_0Y=D[RY1​+(1−R)Y0​]+(1−D)Y0​, so that

E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y1∣X,D=1)=g1(X)+E(U1∣X,D=1)E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y0∣X,D=1)=g0(X)+E(U0∣X,D=1)(5)\begin{aligned} E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=1)&=E(Y_1\mid X,D=1)=g_1(X)+E(U_1\mid X,D=1)\\ E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=0)&=E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)=g_0(X)+E(U_0\mid X,D=1) \end{aligned} \tag{5}E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)​=E(Y1​∣X,D=1)=g1​(X)+E(U1​∣X,D=1)=E(Y0​∣X,D=1)=g0​(X)+E(U0​∣X,D=1)​(5)

and the difference identifies the whole function TT over any subset of the support of XXX given D=1D=1D=1:

E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)−E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)=g1(X)−g0(X)+E(U1−U0∣X,D=1)=E(Δ∣X,D=1)(6)E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=1)-E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=0)=g_1(X)-g_0(X)+E(U_1-U_0\mid X,D=1)=E(\Delta\mid X,D=1) \tag{6}E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)−E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)=g1​(X)−g0​(X)+E(U1​−U0​∣X,D=1)=E(Δ∣X,D=1)(6)

Identifying Assumptions for Matching

Classical matching (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983) assumes conditional independence:

(Y1,Y0)⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥D∣X(7)(Y_1,Y_0)\perp\!\!\!\perp D\mid X \tag{7}(Y1​,Y0​)⊥⊥D∣X(7)

so that F(y0∣X,D=1)=F(y0∣X,D=0)F(y_0\mid X,D=1)=F(y_0\mid X,D=0)F(y0​∣X,D=1)=F(y0​∣X,D=0) and, if the mean exists,

E(Y0∣X,D=1)=E(Y0∣X,D=0)=E(Y0∣X)(8)E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)=E(Y_0\mid X,D=0)=E(Y_0\mid X) \tag{8}E(Y0​∣X,D=1)=E(Y0​∣X,D=0)=E(Y0​∣X)(8)

and the missing counterfactual mean is built from nonparticipants. If in addition

0<Pr⁡(D=1∣X)<1(9)0<\Pr(D=1\mid X)<1 \tag{9}0<Pr(D=1∣X)<1(9)

for all XXX, TT is defined for all XXX; the two together are strong ignorability. For TT and M(S)M(S)M(S) the weaker condition

Y0⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥D∣X(10)Y_0\perp\!\!\!\perp D\mid X \tag{10}Y0​⊥⊥D∣X(10)

is enough, since Y1Y_1Y1​ is observed for participants. Under conditional independence for both Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y0Y_0Y0​, the average treatment effect on a randomly assigned person (ATE) is the weighted average of the effects on the treated and on the untreated:

E(Δ∣X)=Pr⁡(D=1∣X) E(Δ∣X,D=1)+[1−Pr⁡(D=1∣X)]E(Δ∣X,D=0)(11)E(\Delta\mid X)=\Pr(D=1\mid X)\,E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)+\left[1-\Pr(D=1\mid X)\right]E(\Delta\mid X,D=0) \tag{11}E(Δ∣X)=Pr(D=1∣X)E(Δ∣X,D=1)+[1−Pr(D=1∣X)]E(Δ∣X,D=0)(11)

where the effect on the untreated uses Y1⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥D∣XY_1\perp\!\!\!\perp D\mid XY1​⊥⊥D∣X to infer Y1Y_1Y1​ for D=0D=0D=0 from D=1D=1D=1. Matching assumes selection on observables: conditional independence implies Pr⁡(D=1∣X,Y1,Y0)=Pr⁡(D=1∣X)\Pr(D=1\mid X,Y_1,Y_0)=\Pr(D=1\mid X)Pr(D=1∣X,Y1​,Y0​)=Pr(D=1∣X), which rules out Roy-type selection on unobserved potential outcomes, or presumes the analyst knows as much as the agents. To overcome the curse of dimensionality, Rosenbaum and Rubin show that with P(X)=Pr⁡(D=1∣X)P(X)=\Pr(D=1\mid X)P(X)=Pr(D=1∣X), conditional independence and the overlap condition imply (Y1,Y0)⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥D∣P(X)(Y_1,Y_0)\perp\!\!\!\perp D\mid P(X)(Y1​,Y0​)⊥⊥D∣P(X) and hence Y0⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥D∣P(X)Y_0\perp\!\!\!\perp D\mid P(X)Y0​⊥⊥D∣P(X), so matching can be done on the scalar P(X)P(X)P(X) (propensity score sufficiency) if P(X)P(X)P(X) is known. The paper stresses that ignorability is overly strong for mean parameters: all that is required is conditional mean independence in terms of P(X)P(X)P(X),

E(Y0∣P(X),D=1)=E(Y0∣P(X),D=0)(12)E(Y_0\mid P(X),D=1)=E(Y_0\mid P(X),D=0) \tag{12}E(Y0​∣P(X),D=1)=E(Y0​∣P(X),D=0)(12)

which is implied by conditional independence and overlap but can be maintained as a separate and weaker assumption; it restricts only one moment and allows the distribution of Y0Y_0Y0​ to differ in other respects. All theoretical results of the companion paper are derived under it. A further point from the companion paper is that even if P(X)P(X)P(X) were known, conditioning on it can be less efficient than conditioning on XXX itself.

Exclusion Restrictions and Difference-in-Differences

Partition X=(T,Z)X=(T,Z)X=(T,Z), with TTT the variables in the outcome equations and ZZZ those in the participation equation Pr⁡(D=1∣Z)\Pr(D=1\mid Z)Pr(D=1∣Z):

The Bias Function

The bias at a value of XXX from using comparison group outcomes to proxy participants' no-programme outcomes is, in general and in the additively separable case,

B(X)=E(Y0∣X,D=1)−E(Y0∣X,D=0)B(X)=E(U0∣X,D=1)−E(U0∣X,D=0)(16)\begin{aligned} B(X)&=E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)-E(Y_0\mid X,D=0)\\ B(X)&=E(U_0\mid X,D=1)-E(U_0\mid X,D=0) \end{aligned} \tag{16}B(X)B(X)​=E(Y0​∣X,D=1)−E(Y0​∣X,D=0)=E(U0​∣X,D=1)−E(U0​∣X,D=0)​(16)

Earlier work by the authors finds two features. The bias has an index property, B(X)=B~(P(X))B(X)=\tilde{B}(P(X))B(X)=B~(P(X)), consistent with the index-sufficient selection model and the Roy model; if B~(P(X))\tilde{B}(P(X))B~(P(X)) is the same at ttt and t′t't′ (for example, constant over time or symmetric around entry at t=0t=0t=0), the difference-in-differences condition holds with Z=XZ=XZ=X. And the matching assumptions amount to the bias being balanced, B(X)=B~(P(X))=0B(X)=\tilde{B}(P(X))=0B(X)=B~(P(X))=0, which this paper rejects for all four demographic groups. On participation, Heckman and Smith (1994) find that recent unemployment dynamics, not earnings dynamics, best predict who enters JTPA; Ashenfelter's pre-programme earnings dip is a consequence of unemployment spells, and for adult women recent marital transitions also matter.

Common Support and Trimming

Kernel methods require the density of the matching variable to be bounded away from zero. The overlap region is estimated as S^10={P∈S^1∩S^0:f^(P∣D=1)>0 and f^(P∣D=0)>0}\hat{S}_{10}=\{P\in\hat{S}_1\cap\hat{S}_0:\hat{f}(P\mid D=1)>0\text{ and }\hat{f}(P\mid D=0)>0\}S^10​={P∈S^1​∩S^0​:f^​(P∣D=1)>0 and f^​(P∣D=0)>0} with kernel density estimates (Silverman rule-of-thumb bandwidth), and points with very low density are trimmed at level qqq:

Sq={P∈S^10:f^(P∣D=1)>cq and f^(P∣D=0)>cq},sup⁡cq12J∑{i∈Iˉ1}{1(f^(Pi∣D=1)<cq)+1(f^(Pi∣D=0)<cq)}≤q(28)S_q=\left\{P\in\hat{S}_{10}:\hat{f}(P\mid D=1)>c_q\text{ and }\hat{f}(P\mid D=0)>c_q\right\},\qquad\sup_{c_q}\frac{1}{2J}\sum_{\{i\in\bar{I}_1\}}\left\{1\left(\hat{f}(P_i\mid D=1)<c_q\right)+1\left(\hat{f}(P_i\mid D=0)<c_q\right)\right\}\leq q \tag{28}Sq​={P∈S^10​:f^​(P∣D=1)>cq​ and f^​(P∣D=0)>cq​},cq​sup​2J1​{i∈Iˉ1​}∑​{1(f^​(Pi​∣D=1)<cq​)+1(f^​(Pi​∣D=0)<cq​)}≤q(28)

where Iˉ1\bar{I}_1Iˉ1​ is the set of observed PPP values in S^10\hat{S}_{10}S^10​ and JJJ its cardinality; matches are made at control points in S~1∩Sq\tilde{S}_1\cap S_qS~1​∩Sq​, and this region is the SPS_PSP​ of the tables. Restricting to common support changes the parameter: the experiment estimates M(SE)M(S_E)M(SE​) over its full support while the nonexperimental estimator targets M(S10)M(S_{10})M(S10​), and these differ unless SE=S10S_E=S_{10}SE​=S10​.

Data

JTPA Title IIA provides on-the-job training, job search assistance and classroom training to disadvantaged youth and adults, with eligibility based on family income near the poverty line over the previous six months or on welfare and food stamp receipt. In the experiment two thirds of accepted applicants were assigned to treatment and one third randomized out and denied JTPA services for 18 months. ENP data were collected at four of the sixteen sites (Fort Wayne, Corpus Christi, Jersey City and Providence) with the same survey instrument as the controls; baseline and two follow-up surveys (baseline response rate about 84 percent) form a 36-month monthly panel with 18 months before random assignment (or eligibility determination) and 18 months after. The outcome is average monthly earnings over the 18 post-programme months, or quarterly earnings for t=1,…,6t=1,\ldots,6t=1,…,6. Unlike the comparison groups in earlier evaluations (Ashenfelter 1978; Ashenfelter and Card 1985; LaLonde 1986; and others), the ENPs are known to be eligible, live in the same labour markets and have monthly labour force histories. The SIPP comparison group comes from the 1988 panel (October 1987 to December 1989, covering the experiment's random assignment window of November 1987 to September 1989), restricted to JTPA-eligible persons; locations are suppressed, so geographic matching is impossible. No-shows are applicants accepted into the programme who did not enroll. P(X)P(X)P(X) is a logit, weighted for choice-based sampling (Manski and Lerman 1977), whose regressors maximize the within-sample hit rate (classify as a participant if P^(X)\hat{P}(X)P^(X) exceeds the sample participation share). Recent unemployment and labour force transitions are strong predictors for all groups, and earnings in the six months before entry raise the hit rate. All estimates use a bandwidth of 0.06, the biweight kernel, trimming of 2 percent for adults and 5 percent for youth, and 50 bootstrap replications.

Empirical Results

  • Support: the estimated PPP for ENPs is massed near zero while controls spread over the whole unit interval, so the common support is narrow. The shares of controls and ENPs in the overlap region are 60 and 96 percent for adult males, 82 and 96 percent for adult females, 67 and 92 percent for male youth, and 71 and 93 percent for female youth. Experimental impacts are M(SE)=44M(S_E)=44M(SE​)=44, 29, −58-58−58 and −1-1−1 dollars per month for adult males, adult females, male youth and female youth, versus M(SP)=61M(S_P)=61M(SP​)=61, 35, −36-36−36 and 25 on the overlap region, so non-overlap alone shifts the parameter by 17, 6, 22 and 26 dollars (39, 21, 38 and 2500 percent).

  • Bias decomposition (controls vs ENPs): (B^,B^1,B^2,B^3,BˉSP)(\hat{B},\hat{B}_1,\hat{B}_2,\hat{B}_3,\bar{B}_{S_P})(B^,B^1​,B^2​,B^3​,BˉSP​​) equals (−342,218,−584,23,38)(-342,218,-584,23,38)(−342,218,−584,23,38) for adult males, (33,80,−78,31,38)(33,80,-78,31,38)(33,80,−78,31,38) for adult females, (20,142,−131,9,14)(20,142,-131,9,14)(20,142,−131,9,14) for male youth and (42,74,−67,35,49)(42,74,-67,35,49)(42,74,−67,35,49) for female youth. Non-overlap and density weighting are large and offsetting; B^3\hat{B}_3B^3​ is statistically insignificant, but the average selection bias BˉSP\bar{B}_{S_P}BˉSP​​ is 87, 129, 23 and 7239 percent of the experimental impact.

  • Controls vs SIPP: (B^,B^1,B^2,B^3,BˉSP)(\hat{B},\hat{B}_1,\hat{B}_2,\hat{B}_3,\bar{B}_{S_P})(B^,B^1​,B^2​,B^3​,BˉSP​​) equals (−145,151,−417,121,192)(-145,151,-417,121,192)(−145,151,−417,121,192), (47,97,−172,122,198)(47,97,-172,122,198)(47,97,−172,122,198), (−188,65,−263,9,21)(-188,65,-263,9,21)(−188,65,−263,9,21) and (−88,83,−168,−3,−13)(-88,83,-168,-3,-13)(−88,83,−168,−3,−13); for adults the selection component is both absolutely and proportionately larger than with ENPs (440 and 676 percent of the impact).

  • Controls vs no-shows: B^\hat{B}B^ is 29, 9, 84 and 18, smaller than with ENPs for three groups, but its composition shifts toward selection bias (B^23\hat{B}_{23}B^23​ of 38, 18, 91 and 46); for male youth the selection component is large absolutely and proportionately.

  • Tests: conditional independence of Y0Y_0Y0​ is decisively rejected for adult men, rejected at some quantiles of PPP for adult women and female youth, and not rejected for male youth. Overall p-values for conditional mean independence of earnings, pre- and post-programme, are 0.0159 and 0.0000 (adult men), 0.0006 and 0.0000 (adult women), 0.0147 and 0.0251 (male youth), 0.0009 and 0.0000 (female youth); for residuals the post-programme p-values are 0.0001, 0.0008, 0.3561 and 0.0001, so mean independence is rejected except for young males, and pre-programme tests need not agree with post-programme tests (contrary to Heckman and Hotz 1989). The difference-in-differences hypotheses for symmetric quarters are never rejected: overall p-values 0.5260 and 0.4403 (adult males, earnings and residuals), 0.3364 and 0.0506, 0.9832 and 0.9910, 0.0533 and 0.2119.

  • Matching vs ENPs, average bias over t=1,…,6t=1,\ldots,6t=1,…,6: for adult males the raw mean difference is −337-337−337 (775 percent of the impact), nearest neighbour without common support 62, with common support 77, local linear PPP matching 47, regression-adjusted local linear 38, difference-in-differences local linear 67 and regression-adjusted difference-in-differences 52 (120 percent of the impact); the raw bias is almost nine times the impact and seven times the difference-in-differences bias. For adult females the same sequence is 33, 105, 46, 38, 40, 27, 27; for male youth 20, 222, 99, 39, 7, 30, 22; for female youth 48, 102, 37, 61, 8, 52, 17. Imposing common support sharply reduces nearest-neighbour bias except for adult men, local linear does slightly better for youth, and difference-in-differences is often but not uniformly best; biases remain a large share of impacts and vary across quarters. The good average performance of matching reflects offsetting pointwise biases: B(P)B(P)B(P) is substantially negative at low PPP, while the pointwise bias of difference-in-differences is much closer to zero.

  • Conditioning variables: with regression-adjusted local linear matching, the adult male bias is 38 with the regular PPP model but −291-291−291 with demographics only (Coarse I), −166-166−166 adding previous-year earnings (Coarse II) and −25-25−25 adding labour force transitions (Coarse III). The difference-in-differences estimator is less sensitive to the choice of XXX (52, 32, −144-144−144, 43). Matching variables must be good enough to deliver conditional independence but not so good that they predict DDD perfectly, which would destroy overlap.

  • Geography and survey instrument: matching controls with SIPP eligibles gives average biases of 115, 119, 238 and −34-34−34, and difference-in-differences gives −236-236−236, −86-86−86, −28-28−28 and −67-67−67. Matching controls from Providence and Jersey City with ENPs from Corpus Christi and Fort Wayne (same questionnaire, different labour markets) gives −175-175−175, −53-53−53, 33 and 39, while difference-in-differences cuts the adult male bias to −69-69−69, consistent with persistent local labour market effects. Smith (1995) attributes about two thirds of the ENP-SIPP discrepancy to questionnaire differences and the rest to geography. With no-shows, local linear matching gives 25, 7, 99 and 51 and regression-adjusted matching 16, 4, 88 and 49.

The conclusion is that LaLonde's large nonexperimental biases stem mainly from mismatched questionnaires and labour markets and from comparing the incomparable, not from the failure of estimators to remove selection bias; placing comparison persons in the same labour market, using the same questionnaire, and reweighting on a good participation model goes a long way toward replicating an experiment, with regression-adjusted conditional difference-in-differences matching the most robust estimator. The paper also contrasts matching with instrumental variables, which would require E(U0∣X,P,D=1)=E(U0∣X,P,D=0)=0E(U_0\mid X,P,D=1)=E(U_0\mid X,P,D=0)=0E(U0​∣X,P,D=1)=E(U0​∣X,P,D=0)=0, whereas matching requires only that PPP balances the bias.

This is the observation rule of the potential-outcomes (switching regression) model. Every person has two potential outcomes: Y1Y_1Y1​, earnings if trained, and Y0Y_0Y0​, earnings if not trained, both measured in dollars per month in the JTPA application. The indicator D∈{0,1}D\in\{0,1\}D∈{0,1} records which state the person is actually in, and the econometrician sees only the outcome of that state:

Y={Y1if D=1Y0if D=0.Y=\begin{cases} Y_1 & \text{if } D=1\\ Y_0 & \text{if } D=0.\end{cases}Y={Y1​Y0​​if D=1if D=0.​

The individual gain Δ=Y1−Y0\Delta=Y_1-Y_0Δ=Y1​−Y0​ is therefore never observed for anyone, because one of the two terms is always missing. This is the evaluation problem in its purest form: the data reveal E(Y1∣X,D=1)E(Y_1\mid X,D=1)E(Y1​∣X,D=1) and E(Y0∣X,D=0)E(Y_0\mid X,D=0)E(Y0​∣X,D=0) directly, but the parameter of interest, the effect of treatment on the treated in equation (3), also needs the counterfactual E(Y0∣X,D=1)E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)E(Y0​∣X,D=1), which no observational sample contains.

The equation imposes no restriction on how DDD is chosen and allows arbitrary heterogeneity in Δ\DeltaΔ. Everything that follows is about which extra information fills the missing counterfactual: randomization (equations (5) and (6)), conditional independence (equations (7), (8), (10)), mean independence given the propensity score (equation (12)), or a difference-in-differences condition (equations (14) and (15)). The same rule is later extended by the randomization indicator RRR to Y=D[RY1+(1−R)Y0]+(1−D)Y0Y=D[RY_1+(1-R)Y_0]+(1-D)Y_0Y=D[RY1​+(1−R)Y0​]+(1−D)Y0​, so randomized-out controls display Y0Y_0Y0​ although D=1D=1D=1.

Each potential outcome is split into a part explained by observables, gd(X)g_d(X)gd​(X), and a residual UdU_dUd​, d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}d∈{0,1}. Without further assumptions this is only a notation: one can always define gd(X)g_d(X)gd​(X) as any function and Ud=Yd−gd(X)U_d=Y_d-g_d(X)Ud​=Yd​−gd​(X). The content comes from the restrictions imposed on (U1,U0)(U_1,U_0)(U1​,U0​) later.

Conventional econometrics would set gd(X)=Xβdg_d(X)=X\beta_dgd​(X)=Xβd​ and assume E(Ud∣X)=0E(U_d\mid X)=0E(Ud​∣X)=0, so that gdg_dgd​ is the conditional mean and XXX is exogenous. The paper stresses that matching needs neither: gdg_dgd​ need not be linear, and E(Ud∣X)E(U_d\mid X)E(Ud​∣X) need not be zero. What matters for the treatment on the treated is the sum of structure and error means among participants,

E(Yd∣X,D=1)=gd(X)+E(Ud∣X,D=1),E(Y_d\mid X,D=1)=g_d(X)+E(U_d\mid X,D=1),E(Yd​∣X,D=1)=gd​(X)+E(Ud​∣X,D=1),

so selection enters only through E(Ud∣X,D=1)≠E(Ud∣X,D=0)E(U_d\mid X,D=1)\neq E(U_d\mid X,D=0)E(Ud​∣X,D=1)=E(Ud​∣X,D=0). The decomposition becomes substantive in the additively separable case used for regression-adjusted matching: there g0(X)=Xβ0g_0(X)=X\beta_0g0​(X)=Xβ0​ is the same function in both groups, the bias function in equation (16) depends only on the error means, and exclusion restrictions can be stated on U0U_0U0​ alone, as in equation (13). In the JTPA application YdY_dYd​ is monthly earnings and XXX contains demographics, labour force transitions, recent earnings and site indicators.

Start from the definition of the individual gain and substitute equation (2):

Δ=Y1−Y0=[g1(X)+U1]−[g0(X)+U0]=g1(X)−g0(X)+(U1−U0).\Delta=Y_1-Y_0=\left[g_1(X)+U_1\right]-\left[g_0(X)+U_0\right]=g_1(X)-g_0(X)+(U_1-U_0).Δ=Y1​−Y0​=[g1​(X)+U1​]−[g0​(X)+U0​]=g1​(X)−g0​(X)+(U1​−U0​).

Take expectations conditional on XXX and on being a participant, D=1D=1D=1. Since g1(X)g_1(X)g1​(X) and g0(X)g_0(X)g0​(X) are functions of the conditioning variable, they pass through the expectation unchanged:

E(Y1−Y0∣X,D=1)=E(Δ∣X,D=1)=E[g1(X)−g0(X)∣X,D=1]+E(U1−U0∣X,D=1)=g1(X)−g0(X)+E(U1−U0∣X,D=1).\begin{aligned} E(Y_1-Y_0\mid X,D=1)&=E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)\\ &=E\left[g_1(X)-g_0(X)\mid X,D=1\right]+E(U_1-U_0\mid X,D=1)\\ &=g_1(X)-g_0(X)+E(U_1-U_0\mid X,D=1). \end{aligned}E(Y1​−Y0​∣X,D=1)​=E(Δ∣X,D=1)=E[g1​(X)−g0​(X)∣X,D=1]+E(U1​−U0​∣X,D=1)=g1​(X)−g0​(X)+E(U1​−U0​∣X,D=1).​

This is equation (3). The first piece is the structural difference that conventional econometrics targets; the second is the mean of the idiosyncratic gain among those who chose to participate. If people select into training on their unobserved gain, E(U1−U0∣X,D=1)E(U_1-U_0\mid X,D=1)E(U1​−U0​∣X,D=1) differs from the population mean, so TT is a nonstandard parameter combining structure and selection. No exogeneity assumption was used.

M(S)M(S)M(S) averages the pointwise treatment on the treated, equation (3), over a set SSS of XXX values, using the distribution of XXX among participants as weights. The denominator ∫SdF(X∣D=1)=Pr⁡(X∈S∣D=1)\int_S dF(X\mid D=1)=\Pr(X\in S\mid D=1)∫S​dF(X∣D=1)=Pr(X∈S∣D=1) rescales so that the weights integrate to one, hence

M(S)=E(Δ∣X∈S,D=1).M(S)=E(\Delta\mid X\in S,D=1).M(S)=E(Δ∣X∈S,D=1).

If SSS is the whole support of XXX given D=1D=1D=1, this is the unconditional TT, E(Y1−Y0∣D=1)E(Y_1-Y_0\mid D=1)E(Y1​−Y0​∣D=1), in dollars per month. It answers whether participants gained relative to what they would have earned without the programme, and against per-participant costs it tells whether an existing programme should be kept.

The reason for indexing by SSS is support. A nonexperimental estimator can recover E(Δ∣X,D=1)E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)E(Δ∣X,D=1) only where comparable nonparticipants exist, so in practice it estimates M(S10)M(S_{10})M(S10​) or, after trimming, M(SP)M(S_P)M(SP​), while the experiment estimates M(SE)M(S_E)M(SE​) over the full participant support. These are different parameters unless SE=S10S_E=S_{10}SE​=S10​: in the data M(SE)=44M(S_E)=44M(SE​)=44 but M(SP)=61M(S_P)=61M(SP​)=61 for adult males. The matching estimator in equation (21) is the sample analogue of M(S)M(S)M(S), with ωN0,N1(i)=1/N1\omega_{N_0,N_1}(i)=1/N_1ωN0​,N1​​(i)=1/N1​ reproducing the self-weighting by dF(X∣D=1)dF(X\mid D=1)dF(X∣D=1).

The observation rule with randomization among accepted applicants is

Y=D[RY1+(1−R)Y0]+(1−D)Y0.Y=D\left[RY_1+(1-R)Y_0\right]+(1-D)Y_0 .Y=D[RY1​+(1−R)Y0​]+(1−D)Y0​.

Two assumptions are used: compliance (randomized-in persons receive services, randomized-out persons do not), which is built into this rule, and that randomization is independent of potential outcomes within the accepted pool, R⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥(Y1,Y0)∣X,D=1R\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_1,Y_0)\mid X,D=1R⊥⊥(Y1​,Y0​)∣X,D=1.

Condition on D=1D=1D=1 and R=1R=1R=1. The rule gives Y=Y1Y=Y_1Y=Y1​, and independence of RRR lets us drop R=1R=1R=1 from the conditioning set:

E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y1∣X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y1∣X,D=1).E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y_1\mid X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y_1\mid X,D=1).E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y1​∣X,D=1,R=1)=E(Y1​∣X,D=1).

Condition on D=1D=1D=1 and R=0R=0R=0. Now Y=Y0Y=Y_0Y=Y0​, and the same argument gives

E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y0∣X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y0∣X,D=1).E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y_0\mid X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y_0\mid X,D=1).E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y0​∣X,D=1,R=0)=E(Y0​∣X,D=1).

Finally substitute equation (2), with gd(X)g_d(X)gd​(X) passing through the conditional expectation:

E(Yd∣X,D=1)=gd(X)+E(Ud∣X,D=1),d=0,1,E(Y_d\mid X,D=1)=g_d(X)+E(U_d\mid X,D=1),\qquad d=0,1,E(Yd​∣X,D=1)=gd​(X)+E(Ud​∣X,D=1),d=0,1,

which yields both lines of equation (5). The key point is the second line: randomized-out controls reveal the counterfactual mean of participants, which no observational data provide.

Subtract the second line of equation (5) from the first:

E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)−E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)=[g1(X)+E(U1∣X,D=1)]−[g0(X)+E(U0∣X,D=1)]=g1(X)−g0(X)+E(U1−U0∣X,D=1),\begin{aligned} E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=1)-E(Y\mid X,D=1,R=0)&=\left[g_1(X)+E(U_1\mid X,D=1)\right]-\left[g_0(X)+E(U_0\mid X,D=1)\right]\\ &=g_1(X)-g_0(X)+E(U_1-U_0\mid X,D=1), \end{aligned}E(Y∣X,D=1,R=1)−E(Y∣X,D=1,R=0)​=[g1​(X)+E(U1​∣X,D=1)]−[g0​(X)+E(U0​∣X,D=1)]=g1​(X)−g0​(X)+E(U1​−U0​∣X,D=1),​

using linearity of conditional expectation to combine the two error means. By equation (3) the right-hand side is exactly E(Δ∣X,D=1)E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)E(Δ∣X,D=1).

Both conditional means on the left are means of observed outcomes in well-defined subpopulations, so they can be estimated by sample analogues (parametrically or nonparametrically). Since the identity holds at every XXX in the support of XXX given D=1D=1D=1 (randomization guarantees that treatments and controls share that support), one experiment identifies the whole TT function, and integrating against dF(X∣D=1)dF(X\mid D=1)dF(X∣D=1) over any SSS gives M(S)M(S)M(S) of equation (4). This is the benchmark against which the nonexperimental estimators are judged.

Conditional independence says that, among people with the same observables XXX, participation carries no information about potential outcomes: the joint distribution of (Y1,Y0)(Y_1,Y_0)(Y1​,Y0​) is the same for participants and nonparticipants. Equivalently,

Pr⁡(D=1∣X,Y1,Y0)=Pr⁡(D=1∣X),\Pr(D=1\mid X,Y_1,Y_0)=\Pr(D=1\mid X),Pr(D=1∣X,Y1​,Y0​)=Pr(D=1∣X),

so once XXX is controlled for, selection is on observables. This is the identifying assumption of classical matching (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983): it implies equation (8), so nonparticipants with the same XXX supply the missing counterfactual.

Behaviourally the assumption is strong. It rules out Roy-type selection in which people with high unobserved gains U1−U0U_1-U_0U1​−U0​ are more likely to enrol, unless every variable on which agents act is in XXX, i.e. the analyst knows as much as the agents. It is also stronger than needed for TT, which requires only the condition on Y0Y_0Y0​ in equation (10), and for mean parameters only the mean version in equation (12). The paper tests its Y0Y_0Y0​ part directly, because randomized-out controls give the distribution of Y0Y_0Y0​ for D=1D=1D=1: comparing F(y0∣P,D=1)F(y_0\mid P,D=1)F(y0​∣P,D=1) with F(y0∣P,D=0)F(y_0\mid P,D=0)F(y0​∣P,D=0), the hypothesis is decisively rejected for adult men and partly rejected for women and female youth.

Start from conditional independence, equation (7). Joint independence of (Y1,Y0)(Y_1,Y_0)(Y1​,Y0​) and DDD given XXX implies independence of the marginal Y0Y_0Y0​ and DDD given XXX, so the conditional distribution functions coincide:

F(y0∣X,D=1)=F(y0∣X,D=0)for all y0.F(y_0\mid X,D=1)=F(y_0\mid X,D=0)\qquad\text{for all } y_0 .F(y0​∣X,D=1)=F(y0​∣X,D=0)for all y0​.

If the mean exists, integrate y0y_0y0​ against these equal distributions:

E(Y0∣X,D=1)=∫y0 dF(y0∣X,D=1)=∫y0 dF(y0∣X,D=0)=E(Y0∣X,D=0).E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)=\int y_0\,dF(y_0\mid X,D=1)=\int y_0\,dF(y_0\mid X,D=0)=E(Y_0\mid X,D=0).E(Y0​∣X,D=1)=∫y0​dF(y0​∣X,D=1)=∫y0​dF(y0​∣X,D=0)=E(Y0​∣X,D=0).

For the last equality in equation (8), apply the law of iterated expectations over DDD given XXX and use that the two conditional means are equal:

E(Y0∣X)=Pr⁡(D=1∣X)E(Y0∣X,D=1)+[1−Pr⁡(D=1∣X)]E(Y0∣X,D=0)=E(Y0∣X,D=0).\begin{aligned} E(Y_0\mid X)&=\Pr(D=1\mid X)E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)+\left[1-\Pr(D=1\mid X)\right]E(Y_0\mid X,D=0)\\ &=E(Y_0\mid X,D=0). \end{aligned}E(Y0​∣X)​=Pr(D=1∣X)E(Y0​∣X,D=1)+[1−Pr(D=1∣X)]E(Y0​∣X,D=0)=E(Y0​∣X,D=0).​

Only the Y0Y_0Y0​ component of equation (7) was used, so equation (10) suffices. Combined with equation (3), E(Δ∣X,D=1)=E(Y∣X,D=1)−E(Y∣X,D=0)E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)=E(Y\mid X,D=1)-E(Y\mid X,D=0)E(Δ∣X,D=1)=E(Y∣X,D=1)−E(Y∣X,D=0): the counterfactual is built from nonparticipants at the same XXX.

The overlap or common-support condition requires that at every XXX there are both participants and nonparticipants in the population. The upper bound is what matters for TT: if Pr⁡(D=1∣X)=1\Pr(D=1\mid X)=1Pr(D=1∣X)=1 at some XXX, there are no nonparticipants there, E(Y0∣X,D=0)E(Y_0\mid X,D=0)E(Y0​∣X,D=0) is undefined, and equation (8) cannot be used to build the counterfactual. The lower bound ensures that the participant parameter is defined for every XXX. Together with equation (7) it forms strong ignorability, which Rosenbaum and Rubin use to show that matching on P(X)P(X)P(X) alone is valid.

The condition is about the population; its sample counterpart is the main empirical problem of the paper. Estimated participation probabilities of ENPs are massed near zero while controls spread over the whole unit interval, so the estimated overlap set S10S_{10}S10​ is narrow. When overlap fails on part of the support, M(S)M(S)M(S) is identified only for S⊂S10S\subset S_{10}S⊂S10​; the bias decomposition in equations (17) and (18) isolates the cost of ignoring this as B1B_1B1​, and the trimming rule in equation (28) implements overlap in finite samples. A useful special case: if some variable in XXX perfectly predicts participation, Pr⁡(D=1∣X)∈{0,1}\Pr(D=1\mid X)\in\{0,1\}Pr(D=1∣X)∈{0,1} and matching is impossible, which is why better predictors of DDD are not always better matching variables.

This is the weaker independence condition sufficient for the treatment on the treated: only the no-treatment outcome must be independent of participation given XXX. The reason is asymmetric data: Y1Y_1Y1​ of participants is observed, so E(Y1∣X,D=1)E(Y_1\mid X,D=1)E(Y1​∣X,D=1) is identified directly, and the only missing piece of equation (3) is E(Y0∣X,D=1)E(Y_0\mid X,D=1)E(Y0​∣X,D=1), which equation (10) equates to the observable E(Y0∣X,D=0)E(Y_0\mid X,D=0)E(Y0​∣X,D=0), exactly as in the derivation of equation (8).

Compared with equation (7), it allows participation to depend on Y1Y_1Y1​, and hence on the gain Δ\DeltaΔ, given XXX; people may sort on idiosyncratic returns as long as they do not sort on what they would earn untreated. Integrating the identified E(Δ∣X,D=1)E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)E(Δ∣X,D=1) against dF(X∣D=1)dF(X\mid D=1)dF(X∣D=1) on the common support gives M(S)M(S)M(S) of equation (4). For mean parameters one can go further and require only the conditional mean version, equation (12). The symmetric condition Y1⊥ ⁣ ⁣ ⁣⊥D∣XY_1\perp\!\!\!\perp D\mid XY1​⊥⊥D∣X would instead identify the effect on the untreated, used in equation (11).

The identity is the law of iterated expectations applied to Δ\DeltaΔ conditional on XXX, splitting the population at XXX into participants and nonparticipants:

E(Δ∣X)=Pr⁡(D=1∣X) E(Δ∣X,D=1)+Pr⁡(D=0∣X) E(Δ∣X,D=0),E(\Delta\mid X)=\Pr(D=1\mid X)\,E(\Delta\mid X,D=1)+\Pr(D=0\mid X)\,E(\Delta\mid X,D=0),E(Δ∣X)=Pr(D=1∣X)E(Δ∣X,D=1)+Pr(D=0∣X)E(Δ∣X,D=0),

E(Δ∣X,D=0)=E(Y1∣X,D=1)−E(Y0∣X,D=0).E(\Delta\mid X,D=0)=E(Y_1\mid X,D=1)-E(Y_0\mid X,D=0).E(Δ∣X,D=0)=E(Y1​∣X,D=1)−E(Y0​∣X,D=0).

E(Δ)=Pr⁡(D=1) E(Δ∣D=1)+[1−Pr⁡(D=1)]E(Δ∣D=0).E(\Delta)=\Pr(D=1)\,E(\Delta\mid D=1)+\left[1-\Pr(D=1)\right]E(\Delta\mid D=0).E(Δ)=Pr(D=1)E(Δ∣D=1)+[1−Pr(D=1)]E(Δ∣D=0).

This unconditional form is what the paper's footnote 10 describes in words ("weighted average" of TT and the effect on the untreated); the paper prints no formula, and the conditional version in equation (11) is the note author's rendering. It is correct, but under the stated assumption it is a tautology at fixed XXX.

Equation (12) is a primitive assumption in the paper, but it is implied by conditional independence and overlap; we derive that. These are the exclusion-restriction versions of the matching conditions, stated on the outcome residuals. The first line defines the population moment of the conditional difference-in-differences estimator. Add and subtract the counterfactual E(Y0t∣X,D=1)E(Y_{0t}\mid X,D=1)E(Y0t​∣X,D=1) in the participant term:

This is the operational common-support and trimming rule. S^10\hat{S}_{10}S^10​ is the set of PPP values where both kernel density estimates f^(P∣D=1)\hat{f}(P\mid D=1)f^​(P∣D=1) and f^(P∣D=0)\hat{f}(P\mid D=0)f^​(P∣D=0) are positive. Kernel matching estimators need the density of the matching variable to be bounded away from zero; where the comparison density is tiny, a local linear fit rests on one or two observations and is erratic. So points are kept only if both densities exceed a cutoff cqc_qcq​, defining SqS_qSq​.

The cutoff is chosen by a quantile rule. Over the JJJ observed control values Iˉ1\bar{I}_1Iˉ1​ in S^10\hat{S}_{10}S^10​, the average of the two indicators is the fraction of density evaluations that fall below cqc_qcq​ (each point contributes two evaluations, hence 2J2J2J). The paper takes the largest cqc_qcq​ for which this fraction is at most qqq, so approximately a share qqq of low-density evaluations is trimmed:

cq=sup⁡{c:12J∑i∈Iˉ1[1(f^(Pi∣D=1)<c)+1(f^(Pi∣D=0)<c)]≤q}.c_q=\sup\left\{c:\frac{1}{2J}\sum_{i\in\bar{I}_1}\left[1\left(\hat{f}(P_i\mid D=1)<c\right)+1\left(\hat{f}(P_i\mid D=0)<c\right)\right]\leq q\right\}.cq​=sup⎩⎨⎧​c:2J1​i∈Iˉ1​∑​[1(f^​(Pi​∣D=1)<c)+1(f^​(Pi​∣D=0)<c)]≤q⎭⎬⎫​.
